ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Graz (GZ. 39/24/63 ex 2025/26) and was carried out in accordance with all relevant guidelines and regulations.
All participants gave informed consent before participating.
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old and speak a sufficient level of German (native speaker or C1 in the European Language Framework).
table.header: Participants: Recruitment, Exclusion Criteria, and Sample Size

table.text: A total of 382 participants completed the full survey.
table.header: Participants: Recruitment, Exclusion Criteria, and Sample Size

table.text: In the main part of the study, participants were presented with short written health information texts, which either contained correct or incorrect information.
Participants were presented with the items in a randomized order and answered the following questions after each item: "Do you think this information is true or false?"
Before beginning the study, participants provided informed consent to confirm their voluntary participation and understanding of the study's purpose and procedures.

Participants were then asked to provide demographic information concerning their gender, age, nationality, education, place of residence (rural, small town or city), as well as their political orientation and income.
Participants were presented with a total of 50 items of health-related information.
After each item, participants were asked the three questions pertaining to veracity, credibility and prior exposure.
After rating all 50 items, participants were presented with the other questionnaires in the following order: CAM-scale, trust in science, intellectual humility, conspiracy belief and media use.
Items for each scale were randomized We further asked participants if and how distracted they were during the study and what device they used.

Controlling for CR, MFC, and CAM as covariates, intellectual humility had a significant but small association with the credibility ratings, β = 0.024, SE = 0.008, 95% CI [0.008, 0.041], t(338) = 2.87, p = .004 (Supplementary Table S1): More intellectually humble participants gave credibility ratings that were slightly more in line with the scientific evidence.

table.title: Main Study
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.study_design_overview: This study employs a between-subjects design. Health information is presented as trials on 50 pages, which are required to calculate the signal-detection parameters (see Analysis Plan below).
table.randomization: Participants will be provided with the health information texts in random order.
table.data_collection_procedures: Data will be obtained via an online panel provider. Participants are required to be at least 18 years old and speak a sufficient level of German (native speakers or C1 in the European Language Framework). Target quotas are based on current demographic data derived from Statistik Austria (statistik.at). We aim for a quota-representative sample for participants’ age (18-27 years: 13.7%, 28-37 years: 16.7%, 38-47 years: 16.0%, 48-57 years: 17.8%, 58-67 years: 16.4%, 68+ years: 19.4%), gender (appr. 51% female), education (appr. 32% with high school degree), and residential area (appr. 40% rural) and also collect optional data on participant’s political orientation and income.
table.sample_size: For linear models, effect sizes stabilize at a sample size of around N = 250. However, larger samples would be preferable to approach a representative coverage of the population. Following a power calculation in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007, https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03193146), a sample size of N = 350 would be required to detect small effects of one predictor of partial η² = 0.03 (i.e., 3% variance explained; similar to d = 0.34, r = 0.17, β = 0.12, OR = 1.85) with 90% power and an α error level = 0.05 in a two-sided test of a general linear model. We set this sample size as a benchmark for both main effects and two-way interaction effects. We would analyze a minimum of 95% (N = 333) or a maximum of 105% (N = 368) of this sample.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will stop latest after reaching 110% of the anticipated sample (before exclusion), i.e., at N = 385.
table.manipulated_variables: There are no central manipulated variables in this study. The order of the health information varies randomly.
table.measured_variables:
DVs
- accuracy rating (after each health information, 0 = false, 1 = true)
- credibility rating (after each health information, 1 = not at all credible, 7 = highly credible)
There is a total number of 25 correct and 25 incorrect health information pieces (trials), based on evaluations from the fact checking page https://medizin-transparent.at/

IVs (confirmatory and exploratory)
- Cognitive reflection (6 tasks with 4 answer option each; correct answers are counted as 1; based on CRT6 in Toplak et al., 2013, https://doi.org/10.1080/13546783.2013.844729)
- Motivation for cognition (10 items, 1 = “do not agree at all” to 7 “fully agree”, example item: “Right now, I would really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions to problems.”; Blaise et al., 2021, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.785094)
- Public trust in science (5 items, same rating scale, example item: “Scientists can be trusted because they are experienced experts in their particular topic.”; Cologna et al., 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-02090-5)
- Belief in complementary and alternative medicine (6 items, same rating scale, example item: “Complementary medicine should only be used as a last resort when conventional medicine has nothing to offer.” [reversed]; Hyland et al., 2003, https://doi.org/10.1016/s0965-2299(02)00113-9)
- Intellectual humility (6 items, 1 = “does not apply to me at all” to 7 “fully applies to me”, example item: “I question my own opinions, positions, and viewpoints because they could be wrong.”, Schäfer et al., 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2026.113722)
- Conspiracy beliefs (2 items, same rating scale, example item: “Certain significant events have been the result of the activity of a small group who secretly manipulate world events.”, Brohmer et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4230)
- Use of information sources: comprehensive news pages like DerStandard (1 = “every hour”, 7 = “once per month or less”)
- Use of information sources: scientific formats like Kurzgesagt (same rating scale)
- Use of information sources: short video formats on social media (same rating scale)
- Use of information sources: AI (like ChatGPT) for daily routines (same rating scale)
- Use of information sources: AI (like ChatGPT) as source of information (same rating scale)
- Demographic variables (e.g., age, gender, education, residential area, political orientation, income)
- recognition of information pieces (“Did you hear about this health information before?” 0 = no, 1 = yes, 2 = not sure, 3 = I heard the opposite).
table.indices: For the rating scales, we check inter-item correlations and Cronbach’s alpha before calculating the mean composite score. Particularly Cronbach’s alpha should ideally be α = 0.70 (not below 0.60).
table.statistical_tests:
Preprocessing
For each participant an accuracy and a bias score will be calculated according to the signal-detection theory (SDT) approach. Each participant's responses towards the correct and incorrect information in the experimental part will be categorized: Within the “true” (selected) trials, responses will be categorized as “Hits” (for correct information) and “False alarms” (for incorrect information). Within the “false” (selected) trials, responses are categorized as “Misses” (for correct information) and “Correct Rejections” (for incorrect information).
From these answers, each person’s hit rate (H) and the false alarm rate (FA) will be calculated, where the FA rate is the ratio of times a person falsely judged incorrect information as “true” relative to the total number of incorrect information (k = 25), and the H rate is the ratio of “true” ratings relative to the total number of correct information (k = 25). The accuracy value d’ (i.e., sensitivity) is defined as the standardized difference between the means of the signal absent and signal present or in this case “evidence based” (correct) and “not evidence based” (incorrect) trials. d’ is calculated as follows:

 d‘= z(H) – z(FA) 

z(x) is the quantile function for the z distribution such as that a proportion of 0.5 is standardized to a z score of 0. The greater d’ the more accurately a person can distinguish between correct and incorrect health information, whereas d’ values close to zero indicate an inability to distinguish between the information and a chance performance.

The value for response bias is defined as the criterion value c and corresponds to the individual threshold of responding “true” or “false”. c is calculated using the following equation: 

c=-1*(z(H) + z (FA))/2)

A c value of 0 would indicate no bias or preference for responding either “true” or “false”. A lower value would indicate a response bias towards judging information as true or gullibility whereas a higher value would indicate incredulity and being more inclined towards judging information as false.

Analyses
For H1 to H3, we will calculate general linear models with the individual predictors and the DVs accuracy based on d’ (as regression) and credibility ratings (as multilevel model with trials nested in participants) and compare the effect sizes found in the model to the one’s used in the power analysis. We will then conduct general linear models with all predictors together. Only when these predictors remain statistically significant and show effects into the hypothesized direction will this count as robust evidence for their effect.

For H4, we will add relevant IVs and create interaction terms in the respective regression (for accuracy) and multilevel models (for credibility) to analyze potential moderations. Again, we will compare the effects to our power analysis.

RQ3 will be tested as non-directed hypothesis and we apply equivalence testing to test for a potential null effect. To this end, we apply the same effect size estimates as calculated above, but also apply two one-sided tests (i.e., 90% confidence intervals) to test effects equivalent to zero.
table.transformations: Beside the transformation described in the preprocessing part above, we need to calculate an information-adjusted credibility rating: the minimum and maximum credibility rating will be coded in way that higher scores represent correct answers in line with scientific evidence. That is, if a correct information is rated with maximum credibility (“7”), it keeps this score. If an incorrect information is rated with maximum credibility, it receives a “1” (and vice versa).
table.inference_criteria: We conduct statistical tests and check their p-values. Also, we will look at the effect sizes as indicated in the power analysis. Effects from zero-order models (i.e., without covariates) that reach the effect sizes from the power analysis (i.e., their 95% confidence interval overlaps with the threshold) and that are p < .05 will count as evidence in favor of an effect.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We automatically exclude participants, when their quota is already full, and who fail the attention check that we included in the health information part: After 10 health information trials, they will be asked, which health information they saw on the last page and need to select the correct answer (out of 5 answer options). 
We will further exclude participants, who indicated at the end that they got distracted during the survey (3 on a scale from 1 = “not at all” to 4 = “all the time”), who straight-lined the items for the predictor variables (i.e., they have SD = 0), and who answered the whole survey in less than 15 minutes (which equates to participants answering each health information in 15 seconds and the other questions in less than 3 minutes).
table.missing_data_handling: We do not expect further missing data, but will exclude those, who do not fill out all 50 health information items or show unusual responses (e.g., more than one missing value on predictor items).
table.exploratory_analyses:
First, we want to test the effects of further individual difference variables, including conspiracy theoretical thinking, and general trust in science.
How is participants’ … related to accuracy and the credibility ratings?
RQ4: degree of conspiracy belief 
RQ5: general trust in science 

Participants further consume different media and information sources in their everyday life. These habits may affect their reception of health information too:
To what degree is participants’ receptivity of … related to accuracy and credibility ratings?
RQ6: scientific content 
RQ7: extensive news and reporting
RQ8: entertaining short video formats
RQ9: AI in everyday tasks
RQ10: AI as source of information

People might differ in their skill level when looking at correct and incorrect information separately (i.e., in their response bias c). For example, it might be possible that certain people are good at recognizing correct information as true but when confronted with incorrect information they might be guessing. Hence, we formulate:
RQ11: Which individual differences affect people's response bias c’ when it comes to evaluating evidence-based health information and health information contrary to the scientific evidence?

To differentiate this further, we want to test another exploratory approach to more comprehensively describe the population by grouping people according to their responses towards information: The possible response patterns for i) correct or ii) incorrect information are either 1) random guessing, 2) being better than random guessing, and 3) being worse than random guessing (or opposite to the scientific evidence). This yields 32 = 9 possible combinations for people’s response pattern. These groups can also be represented by their combinations of d’ and c values, which are conceptually plotted in Figure P1: https://osf.io/syd5u/files/b63ug?view_only=936fda8346d44ecfbcc5a1473afd15d4

We will describe the Austrian population by determining the percentages of each group. This is expected to give valuable information about where interventions might be most effective. In a further step we want to determine if any of the individual differences assessed in this study can be used to predict group membership by conducting a multinominal logistic regression analysis with the groups as DV and the predictors above as IVs.
RQ12: How do individual differences predict the group membership?

We will check if credibility ratings for information that people heard of before could be higher than for unknown information, independent of whether the information are correct or incorrect. We will use the two relevant groups (known before and not known before) and the two categories of health information (correct and incorrect) and compare the credibility ratings for each health information between these groups.
RQ13: Does previous knowledge of the information increases the likelihood to indicate that it is perceived as true?
table.research_questions:
Here, we present our Research Questions (RQs) and Hypotheses (H). 
RQ 1: Which individual differences of people are associated with their accuracy (i.e., correctly detecting right and wrong information) and credibility ratings in regard to the evaluation of evidence-based (i.e., correct) health information and non-evidence-based (i.e., incorrect) health information?
H1: Higher scores in cognitive reflection are positively associated with a) accuracy and b) information-adjusted credibility ratings.
H2: More motivation for cognition is positively associated with a) accuracy and b) information-adjusted credibility ratings.
H3: Positive attitudes towards alternative medicine is negatively associated with a) accuracy and b) information-adjusted credibility ratings.

RQ 2: Do positive attitudes toward alternative medicine moderate the positive associations with the other predictor variables?
H4: Higher attitudes towards alternative medicine attenuate the positive association of cognitive reflection (a, b) and motivation for cognition (c, d) with accuracy and credibility, respectively.

RQ 3: How does intellectual humility relate to accuracy and credibility?
As the direction of this research question is not clear, no precise hypotheses will be formulated. It could be that intellectual humble people are less certain when making decisions on health information (i.e., less extreme ratings), but their reasoning could also lead to more accurate judgements.

Further exploratory RQs are formulated below.

IVs (confirmatory and exploratory)

- Motivation for cognition (10 items, 1 = “do not agree at all” to 7 “fully agree”, example item: “Right now, I would really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions to problems.”; Blaise et al., 2021, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.785094)
- Public trust in science (5 items, same rating scale, example item: “Scientists can be trusted because they are experienced experts in their particular topic.”; Cologna et al., 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-02090-5)
- Belief in complementary and alternative medicine (6 items, same rating scale, example item: “Complementary medicine should only be used as a last resort when conventional medicine has nothing to offer.” [reversed]; Hyland et al., 2003, https://doi.org/10.1016/s0965-2299(02)00113-9)
- Intellectual humility (6 items, 1 = “does not apply to me at all” to 7 “fully applies to me”, example item: “I question my own opinions, positions, and viewpoints because they could be wrong.”, Schäfer et al., 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2026.113722)
- Conspiracy beliefs (2 items, same rating scale, example item: “Certain significant events have been the result of the activity of a small group who secretly manipulate world events.”, Brohmer et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4230)

- Use of information sources: short video formats on social media (same rating scale)

Particularly Cronbach’s alpha should ideally be α = 0.70 (not below 0.60).", "Preprocessing
For each participant an accuracy and a bias score will be calculated according to the signal-detection theory (SDT) approach. Each participant's responses towards the correct and incorrect information in the experimental part will be categorized: Within the “true” (selected) trials, responses will be categorized as “Hits” (for correct information) and “False alarms” (for incorrect information). Within the “false” (selected) trials, responses are categorized as “Misses” (for correct information) and “Correct Rejections” (for incorrect information).
From these answers, each person’s hit rate (H) and the false alarm rate (FA) will be calculated, where the FA rate is the ratio of times a person falsely judged incorrect information as “true” relative to the total number of incorrect information (k = 25), and the H rate is the ratio of “true” ratings relative to the total number of correct information (k = 25). The accuracy value d’ (i.e., sensitivity) is defined as the standardized difference between the means of the signal absent and signal present or in this case “evidence based” (correct) and “not evidence based” (incorrect) trials. d’ is calculated as follows:

d‘= z(H) – z(FA)

z(x) is the quantile function for the z distribution such as that a proportion of 0.5 is standardized to a z score of 0. The greater d’ the more accurately a person can distinguish between correct and incorrect health information, whereas d’ values close to zero indicate an inability to distinguish between the information and a chance performance.

The value for response bias is defined as the criterion value c and corresponds to the individual threshold of responding “true” or “false”. c is calculated using the following equation:

c=-1*(z(H) + z (FA))/2)

A c value of 0 would indicate no bias or preference for responding either “true” or “false”. A lower value would indicate a response bias towards judging information as true or gullibility whereas a higher value would indicate incredulity and being more inclined towards judging information as false.

Analyses
For H1 to H3, we will calculate general linear models with the individual predictors and the DVs accuracy based on d’ (as regression) and credibility ratings (as multilevel model with trials nested in participants) and compare the effect sizes found in the model to the one’s used in the power analysis. We will then conduct general linear models with all predictors together. Only when these predictors remain statistically significant and show effects into the hypothesized direction will this count as robust evidence for their effect.

For H4, we will add relevant IVs and create interaction terms in the respective regression (for accuracy) and multilevel models (for credibility) to analyze potential moderations. Again, we will compare the effects to our power analysis.

RQ3 will be tested as non-directed hypothesis and we apply equivalence testing to test for a potential null effect. To this end, we apply the same effect size estimates as calculated above, but also apply two one-sided tests (i.e., 90% confidence intervals) to test effects equivalent to zero.", "Beside the transformation described in the preprocessing part above, we need to calculate an information-adjusted credibility rating: the minimum and maximum credibility rating will be coded in way that higher scores represent correct answers in line with scientific evidence. That is, if a correct information is rated with maximum credibility (“7”), it keeps this score. If an incorrect information is rated with maximum credibility, it receives a “1” (and vice versa).", "We conduct statistical tests and check their p-values. Also, we will look at the effect sizes as indicated in the power analysis. Effects from zero-order models (i.e., without covariates) that reach the effect sizes from the power analysis (i.e., their 95% confidence interval overlaps with the threshold) and that are p < .05 will count as evidence in favor of an effect.", "We automatically exclude participants, when their quota is already full, and who fail the attention check that we included in the health information part: After 10 health information trials, they will be asked, which health information they saw on the last page and need to select the correct answer (out of 5 answer options).
We will further exclude participants, who indicated at the end that they got distracted during the survey (3 on a scale from 1 = “not at all” to 4 = “all the time”), who straight-lined the items for the predictor variables (i.e., they have SD = 0), and who answered the whole survey in less than 15 minutes (which equates to participants answering each health information in 15 seconds and the other questions in less than 3 minutes).", "We do not expect further missing data, but will exclude those, who do not fill out all 50 health information items or show unusual responses (e.g., more than one missing value on predictor items).", "First, we want to test the effects of further individual difference variables, including conspiracy theoretical thinking, and general trust in science.
How is participants’ … related to accuracy and the credibility ratings?
RQ4: degree of conspiracy belief
RQ5: general trust in science

Participants further consume different media and information sources in their everyday life. These habits may affect their reception of health information too:
To what degree is participants’ receptivity of … related to accuracy and credibility ratings?
RQ6: scientific content
RQ7: extensive news and reporting

People might differ in their skill level when looking at correct and incorrect information separately (i.e., in their response bias c). For example, it might be possible that certain people are good at recognizing correct information as true but when confronted with incorrect information they might be guessing. Hence, we formulate:
RQ11: Which individual differences affect people's response bias c’ when it comes to evaluating evidence-based health information and health information contrary to the scientific evidence?

To differentiate this further, we want to test another exploratory approach to more comprehensively describe the population by grouping people according to their responses towards information: The possible response patterns for i) correct or ii) incorrect information are either 1) random guessing, 2) being better than random guessing, and 3) being worse than random guessing (or opposite to the scientific evidence). This yields 32 = 9 possible combinations for people’s response pattern. These groups can also be represented by their combinations of d’ and c values, which are conceptually plotted in Figure P1: https://osf.io/syd5u/files/b63ug?view_only=936fda8346d44ecfbcc5a1473afd15d4

We will describe the Austrian population by determining the percentages of each group. This is expected to give valuable information about where interventions might be most effective. In a further step we want to determine if any of the individual differences assessed in this study can be used to predict group membership by conducting a multinominal logistic regression analysis with the groups as DV and the predictors above as IVs.
RQ12: How do individual differences predict the group membership?

We will check if credibility ratings for information that people heard of before could be higher than for unknown information, independent of whether the information are correct or incorrect. We will use the two relevant groups (known before and not known before) and the two categories of health information (correct and incorrect) and compare the credibility ratings for each health information between these groups.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Careless Responding

475 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **451 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed 2 self-reproducible output files (JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/Mplus) instead of R code.
-  4502 statistics stored from the extracted output.
-  40 of 49 reported tests matched (81.6%).
-  We found no R or Python code files to assess for reproducibility.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Graz (GZ. 39/24/63 ex 2025/26) and was carried out in accordance with all relevant guidelines and regulations.
live_data_statements: All participants gave informed consent before participating.
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old and speak a sufficient level of German (native speaker or C1 in the European Language Framework).
A total of 382 participants completed the full survey.
In the main part of the study, participants were presented with short written health information texts, which either contained correct or incorrect information.
Participants were presented with the items in a randomized order and answered the following questions after each item: "Do you think this information is true or false?"
Before beginning the study, participants provided informed consent to confirm their voluntary participation and understanding of the study's purpose and procedures.

Participants were then asked to provide demographic information concerning their gender, age, nationality, education, place of residence (rural, small town or city), as well as their political orientation and income.
Participants were presented with a total of 50 items of health-related information.
After each item, participants were asked the three questions pertaining to veracity, credibility and prior exposure.
After rating all 50 items, participants were presented with the other questionnaires in the following order: CAM-scale, trust in science, intellectual humility, conspiracy belief and media use.
Items for each scale were randomized We further asked participants if and how distracted they were during the study and what device they used.

Controlling for CR, MFC, and CAM as covariates, intellectual humility had a significant but small association with the credibility ratings, β = 0.024, SE = 0.008, 95% CI [0.008, 0.041], t(338) = 2.87, p = .004 (Supplementary Table S1): More intellectually humble participants gave credibility ratings that were slightly more in line with the scientific evidence.
Most of our participants showed a liberal response bias, that is, a tendency to judge information as "true" regardless of its veracity.

report: #### Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

2 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 140 result tables (4502 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.
#### Reported vs. reproduced
49 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 40 matched (36 fully, 4 partially) — 81.6% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

info.title: Prior Beliefs not Cognitive Reflection Predict People's Accuracy when Judging Health (Mis)Information

text.text: Health misinformation affects individual and public health decisions and erodes trust in medical institutions.
Online, people are often confronted with a large variety of both evidencebased and misleading content, making credibility assessments challenging.
Judgment errors are not simply the result of a lack of access to accurate information but depend on a variety of cognitive, social and affective factors.
In this study, we asked a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population (N = 343) to assess the veracity and credibility of 50 health claims drawn from real-world online information.
Using a signal-detection approach, we examined which individual differences predicted accuracy, perceived credibility and response bias.

Results indicate that stronger belief in alternative medicine and in conspiracy theories were associated with lower accuracy, whereas cognitive reflection, motivation for cognition and intellectual humility were not.
Stronger belief in alternative medicine, more trust in science, and older age were also associated with being more likely to believe any information regardless of veracity.
Overall, our results point towards prior beliefs, not cognitive variables, playing a larger role in what information people choose to believe.
Implications for interventions are discussed.
When people turn to the internet for information about their health, a large share of what they find may be wrong.

This is especially true on social media, where content audits estimate that, depending on platform and topic, between roughly 30% and 87% of health-related social media posts contain misinformation [1].
text.formatted: This is especially true on social media, where content audits estimate that, depending on platform and topic, between roughly 30% and 87% of health-related social media posts contain misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Exposure to misinformation carries real consequences: misleading claims can negatively influence individual health decisions [2], and more broadly endanger public health, e.g., by undermining vaccination intentions [3], and erode trust in medicine and health institutions [4].
text.formatted: Exposure to misinformation carries real consequences: misleading claims can negatively influence individual health decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, and more broadly endanger public health, e.g., by undermining vaccination intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, and erode trust in medicine and health institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Exposure alone, however, does not automatically equal believing wrong information.
Two people can view the same claim-say a post claiming that vaccines cause autism (a longdebunked claim [5, 6])-and reach completely opposite conclusions regarding its veracity.
text.formatted: Two people can view the same claim-say a post claiming that vaccines cause autism (a longdebunked claim <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>)-and reach completely opposite conclusions regarding its veracity.

text.text: The psychological processes behind this divergence are still not properly understood, though a large variety of cognitive, social, and affective factors have been proposed [7].
text.formatted: The psychological processes behind this divergence are still not properly understood, though a large variety of cognitive, social, and affective factors have been proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Many interventions have been developed to counter misinformation, but evidence for their effectiveness and real-world usability remains mixed [8, 9].
text.formatted: Many interventions have been developed to counter misinformation, but evidence for their effectiveness and real-world usability remains mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: This could be because errors in judging information can have a large variety of different causes, such as limited health literacy, and a variety of cognitive biases and fallacies (e.g., illusory truth effects [7]), but also a general tendency to overtrust information or excessive skepticism.
text.formatted: This could be because errors in judging information can have a large variety of different causes, such as limited health literacy, and a variety of cognitive biases and fallacies (e.g., illusory truth effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>), but also a general tendency to overtrust information or excessive skepticism.

text.text: To design better interventions, we need to identify not just who is more likely to be fooled (i.e., which individual differences are associated with errors, such as lower cognitive reflection or stronger belief in alternative medicine), but also how: Do they struggle to tell true from false claims, or do they have a general disposition to accept (overtrust) or reject (skepticism) claims regardless of veracity?

In the present work, we assess the ability of the Austrian population to evaluate a wide range of health (mis)information correctly, using a signal-detection theory (SDT) approach, which addresses both questions.

Many misinformation studies use simple scores, such as counting correctly answered items, which conflates whether people can tell true from false claims with their general tendency to accept or reject information [10].
text.formatted: Many misinformation studies use simple scores, such as counting correctly answered items, which conflates whether people can tell true from false claims with their general tendency to accept or reject information <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Because laypeople often lack the knowledge to be sure whether a claim is true, judging online information resembles a signal-detection paradigm, since both involve decisions under uncertainty.

A SDT framework allows us to separate two otherwise entangled, distinct aspects: People's ability to discriminate true from false information (d'; hereafter accuracy) and their general response bias (c), the general tendency to accept versus reject claims.

This distinction has direct practical implications: People with low d′ might benefit from interventions that foster analytic engagement and structured evaluation (e.g., accuracy-nudge interventions [11]), whereas a shifted c might call for threshold recalibration: an overly conservative criterion, for instance, risks rejecting accurate health information whereas an overly liberal one risks accepting misinformation [12].
text.formatted: This distinction has direct practical implications: People with low d′ might benefit from interventions that foster analytic engagement and structured evaluation (e.g., accuracy-nudge interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>), whereas a shifted c might call for threshold recalibration: an overly conservative criterion, for instance, risks rejecting accurate health information whereas an overly liberal one risks accepting misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Dual-process models have a long tradition in psychology (e.g., [13] [14] [15]) and are frequently used to explain why people diverge in their judgments of misinformation [16] [17] [18].
text.formatted: Dual-process models have a long tradition in psychology (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>) and are frequently used to explain why people diverge in their judgments of misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: These models propose that judgments can rely either on heuristic, peripheral, or intuitive processing (such as surface markers, source familiarity, or prior attitudes), or on a more effortful and reflective evaluation of the content [19].
text.formatted: These models propose that judgments can rely either on heuristic, peripheral, or intuitive processing (such as surface markers, source familiarity, or prior attitudes), or on a more effortful and reflective evaluation of the content <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: According to the Elaboration-Likelihood Model [15], whether a person engages the effortful pathway depends jointly on their ability and their motivation to do so.
text.formatted: According to the Elaboration-Likelihood Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, whether a person engages the effortful pathway depends jointly on their ability and their motivation to do so.

text.text: Applied to misinformation, both are generally assumed to improve accuracy.

Consistent with the ability side, performance on the cognitive reflection test (CRT) was positively associated with the ability to discern true from false information in many domains, such as US political news [17], COVID-19 headlines [20], and claims about Russia and Ukraine [21].
text.formatted: Consistent with the ability side, performance on the cognitive reflection test (CRT) was positively associated with the ability to discern true from false information in many domains, such as US political news <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, COVID-19 headlines <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, and claims about Russia and Ukraine <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: To capture the motivation side, it is important to consider motivation for cognition (MFC), people's momentary motivation to engage in effortful thinking [22].
text.formatted: To capture the motivation side, it is important to consider motivation for cognition (MFC), people's momentary motivation to engage in effortful thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: MFC is the state counterpart of the trait need for cognition [23], which has been linked to better detection of fake news [24].
text.formatted: MFC is the state counterpart of the trait need for cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>, which has been linked to better detection of fake news <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Analytic thinking also reduced unfounded beliefs only among people who were at the same time motivated to hold rational beliefs [25].
text.formatted: Analytic thinking also reduced unfounded beliefs only among people who were at the same time motivated to hold rational beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Even prompting people to think about accuracy, which may shift their momentary motivation toward accuracy, made them better at distinguishing true from false headlines when deciding what to share [26].
text.formatted: Even prompting people to think about accuracy, which may shift their momentary motivation toward accuracy, made them better at distinguishing true from false headlines when deciding what to share <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: However, this relationship is not always straightforward.

Higher need for cognition, for instance, was also associated with stronger belief in the content of conspiracy-theoretical social media posts [27], and a similar pattern emerged for health misinformation among people who relied on social media or alternative health media [28].
text.formatted: Higher need for cognition, for instance, was also associated with stronger belief in the content of conspiracy-theoretical social media posts <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>, and a similar pattern emerged for health misinformation among people who relied on social media or alternative health media <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that prior beliefs also shape how accurately people judge information.
Particularly relevant for health information are belief in alternative medicine, conspiracy beliefs, and trust in science.
People tend to accept information that fits their prior beliefs and to doubt information that does not.

In political fake news research, partisan biases are well documented: news that is congruent with people's political orientation (e.g., pro-Republican news for conservatives) is accepted more readily than incongruent news [10, 12].
text.formatted: In political fake news research, partisan biases are well documented: news that is congruent with people's political orientation (e.g., pro-Republican news for conservatives) is accepted more readily than incongruent news <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: Similar effects occur beyond politics: for topics such as gender-sensitive language and complementary and alternative medicine, laypeople trust study results that conform to their prior beliefs more, while explicit quality signals (e.g., Open Science practices) have no effect [29].
text.formatted: Similar effects occur beyond politics: for topics such as gender-sensitive language and complementary and alternative medicine, laypeople trust study results that conform to their prior beliefs more, while explicit quality signals (e.g., Open Science practices) have no effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Beliefs about alternative medicine are of particular interest in the context of health information.

While some beliefs are relatively harmless, the extreme end of alternative medicine and "natural" healing methods often coincides with a rejection of evidence-based practices, in German derogatorily called "Schulmedizin" (roughly, "conventional mainstream medicine").
Many practices of alternative medicine lack evidence of efficacy [30].
text.formatted: Many practices of alternative medicine lack evidence of efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Such beliefs can be assumed to be related to lower accuracy.
Consistent with this, positive attitudes towards alternative medicine were among the strongest predictors of susceptibility to health misinformation [31].
text.formatted: Consistent with this, positive attitudes towards alternative medicine were among the strongest predictors of susceptibility to health misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Another relevant factor may be conspiracy belief: a general disposition to interpret events as the result of malevolent agents or hidden agency [32].
text.formatted: Another relevant factor may be conspiracy belief: a general disposition to interpret events as the result of malevolent agents or hidden agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: A typical health-related example is the claim that authorities and pharmaceutical companies conceal the dangers of vaccines [33].
text.formatted: A typical health-related example is the claim that authorities and pharmaceutical companies conceal the dangers of vaccines <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: A conspiratorial worldview has also been associated with lower belief in scientific media content [27], so conspiracy belief may be related to lower accuracy.
text.formatted: A conspiratorial worldview has also been associated with lower belief in scientific media content <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>, so conspiracy belief may be related to lower accuracy.

text.text: Finally, people who trust in science should be more likely to follow and believe evidencebased information and thus be more accurate.

Consistent with this, higher trust in scientists was associated with lower susceptibility to COVID-19 misinformation [34], and distrust in the health care system predicted greater susceptibility to health misinformation [31].
text.formatted: Consistent with this, higher trust in scientists was associated with lower susceptibility to COVID-19 misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>, and distrust in the health care system predicted greater susceptibility to health misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, the importance of beliefs and attitudes points to a limitation of dual-process accounts which largely make lack of reasoning responsible for misjudgments.
Yet it is unlikely that people who believe in alternative medicine or conspiracy theories never apply reasoning.

In fact, such beliefs are often accompanied by elaborate (if extremely flawed) argumentation: Alternative healing systems, such as homeopathy, rest on extensive theoretical writings (e.g., Hahnemann's writings on homeopathy), and conspiracy theories can be highly complex [35].
text.formatted: In fact, such beliefs are often accompanied by elaborate (if extremely flawed) argumentation: Alternative healing systems, such as homeopathy, rest on extensive theoretical writings (e.g., Hahnemann's writings on homeopathy), and conspiracy theories can be highly complex <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Under motivated reasoning [36], reasoning is directed toward a desired conclusion.
text.formatted: Under motivated reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>, reasoning is directed toward a desired conclusion.

text.text: Whether this happens when people judge misinformation is debated.

Analytic thinking has mostly predicted better discernment, regardless of alignment with participants' own political ideology [17], whereas partisan bias has also been a strong predictor of misinformation susceptibility [37].
text.formatted: Analytic thinking has mostly predicted better discernment, regardless of alignment with participants' own political ideology <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, whereas partisan bias has also been a strong predictor of misinformation susceptibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: This raises the possibility that prior beliefs and cognition do not simply add together in predicting accuracy but can interact: for someone who holds strong beliefs about alternative medicine, cognitive reasoning might not correct wrong beliefs but confirm them further.
A further trait that may affect how people judge health information is intellectual humility: an awareness of the limits of one's own knowledge, and uncertainty about one's own beliefs [38].
text.formatted: A further trait that may affect how people judge health information is intellectual humility: an awareness of the limits of one's own knowledge, and uncertainty about one's own beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>.

text.text: In the political domain, it is related to higher openness to the opposing view [38] and predicts more investigative behavior, such as fact checking, in response to information [39].
text.formatted: In the political domain, it is related to higher openness to the opposing view <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> and predicts more investigative behavior, such as fact checking, in response to information <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: Its direct relationship to judgments about health information, however, is less clear.
It might act as a protective factor, where intellectually humble individuals are more accurate, but they might equally be less certain in their judgments overall.
So far, we have mainly discussed how individual differences might relate to accuracy, as correct discrimination is often the goal when it comes to health information.
Some of these individual differences might, however, also affect how readily people accept or reject claims in general, captured by the response bias (c).
Most misinformation research has focused solely on accuracy [40] and, to our knowledge, few studies have examined which individual differences relate to response bias.
text.formatted: Most misinformation research has focused solely on accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> and, to our knowledge, few studies have examined which individual differences relate to response bias.

text.text: One study found that, for political news, partisan bias was unrelated to discrimination ability and had different correlates, such as subjective confidence instead of cognitive reflection [37].
text.formatted: One study found that, for political news, partisan bias was unrelated to discrimination ability and had different correlates, such as subjective confidence instead of cognitive reflection <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: Another study found that for political and COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, discrimination ability was related to, for example, cognitive reflection and conspiracy mentality, whereas the acceptance threshold showed no robust associations with any of 15 individual difference dimensions [41].
text.formatted: Another study found that for political and COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, discrimination ability was related to, for example, cognitive reflection and conspiracy mentality, whereas the acceptance threshold showed no robust associations with any of 15 individual difference dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: A comparable study found only small associations between individual differences and response bias [20].
text.formatted: A comparable study found only small associations between individual differences and response bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: For health information beyond COVID-19, however, little is known about this.
We therefore examine the relationship between the response bias c and all assessed individual differences in an exploratory way.
Most research on misinformation has focused on political misinformation, often in a US context, with comparatively little work on health information (especially beyond COVID- 19) or non-US samples.
text.formatted: Most research on misinformation has focused on political misinformation, often in a US context, with comparatively little work on health information (especially beyond COVID- <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19)</ref> or non-US samples.

text.text: In the present study, we investigated individual differences in the ability to discern true and false health information across a large variety of health information contexts in the Austrian population.

Based on dual-process accounts, we expected higher cognitive reflection (H1) and higher motivation for cognition (H2) to be associated with higher accuracy and more appropriate credibility ratings, and more positive attitudes towards alternative medicine to be associated with lower accuracy and less appropriate credibility ratings (H3).

In line with motivated reasoning, we further expected belief in alternative medicine to attenuate the positive associations of cognitive reflection and motivation for cognition with accuracy and credibility (H4).

For all other predictors, we preregistered open research questions: how intellectual humility, conspiracy belief, and trust in science relate to accuracy and credibility (RQ3-RQ5), which individual differences are associated with response bias (RQ6), and which response patterns to correct and incorrect health information can be distinguished and how individual differences predict them (RQ7).
The preregistered hypotheses and full research questions are listed in the Methods.
This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) https://osf.io/prt76/overview?view_only=2409483a31c1491eb43996dc6e15c159.
text.formatted: This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/prt76/overview?view_only=2409483a31c1491eb43996dc6e15c159">https://osf.io/prt76/overview?view_only=2409483a31c1491eb43996dc6e15c159</ref>.

text.text: We defined the following research questions (RQs) that are relevant for this paper, along with confirmatory hypotheses (Hs): RQ2: Do positive attitudes toward alternative medicine moderate the positive associations with the other predictor variables?
H4: More positive attitudes towards alternative medicine attenuate the positive association of cognitive reflection and motivation for cognition with accuracy and credibility, respectively.
We further formulated exploratory research questions, which are as follows:
RQ3: How does intellectual humility relate to accuracy and credibility ratings?
RQ4: How is participants' degree of conspiracy belief related to the accuracy and credibility ratings?
RQ5: How is participants' general trust in science related to accuracy and credibility ratings?
RQ6: Which individual differences affect people's response bias c when it comes to evaluating evidence-based health information and health information contrary to the scientific evidence?
Accuracy and bias summarize performance across all items, but people may also differ in how they respond to correct and incorrect information separately, which is not shown by either index alone.
Some people might, for example, reliably recognize correct information as true but guess when confronted with incorrect information.
We preregistered an approach on how to group people according to response patterns and accordingly formulated RQ7 to describe the population in more detail.
Which response patterns to correct and incorrect health information can be distinguished in the Austrian population, and how do individual differences predict them?
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Graz (GZ. 39/24/63 ex 2025/26) and was carried out in accordance with all relevant guidelines and regulations.
All participants gave informed consent before participating.
Participant recruitment took place via the panel provider Talk Online (https://talkonlinepanel.com/) to achieve a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population.
text.formatted: Participant recruitment took place via the panel provider Talk Online (<ref type="url" target="https://talkonlinepanel.com/">https://talkonlinepanel.com</ref>) to achieve a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population.

text.text: Participants were required to be at least 18 years old and speak a sufficient level of German (native speaker or C1 in the European Language Framework).
Our target quotas were based on current demographic data derived from Statistik Austria (http://statistik.at/).
text.formatted: Our target quotas were based on current demographic data derived from Statistik Austria (<ref type="url" target="http://statistik.at/">statistik.at</ref>).

text.text: Quotas were set for participants' age (18-27 years: 13.7%, 28-37 years: 16.7%, 38-47 years: 16.0%, 48-57 years: 17.8%, 58-67 years: 16.4%, 68+ years: 19.4%), gender (approx. 51% female), education (approx. 32% with high school degree or higher), and residential area (approx. 40% rural).
We also collected data on participants' political orientation (from "1 -very left", "6 -center", "11 -very right") and net income ("under 1600€", "over 1600€", "over 2300 €", and "over 3000€").
In our preregistration data collection was set to stop at N = 385 (110% of the anticipated sample) prior to exclusion.

Following a power calculation in G*Power [42] we aimed for a sample size of N = 350 to detect small effects (corresponding to η² = 0.03, i.e., 3% variance explained; similar to d = 0.34, r = 0.17, β = 0.12, OR = 1.85; [43]) of individual predictors with 90% power at an α error level = 0.05 in a two-sided test in a general linear model.

text.text: We aimed to analyze between a minimum of 95% (N = 333) and a maximum of 105% (N = 368) of this sample.
A total of 382 participants completed the full survey.

According to our preregistration we excluded participants who completed the survey in less than 15 minutes, straight-lined a main questionnaire with reversed items (MFC and HCAMQ), failed the attention check and who self-reported in the end that they got distracted "every so often" or "all the time" during the survey.
For our final data analysis, N = 343 remained, which was inside the anticipated range.

Our final sample had an average age of M = 50.51 years (SD = 18.20; min = 18; max = 87), 51.9% were male, 33.6% had a high school (Matura) or university degree, and 42.0% lived in the countryside (less than 10,000 inhabitants in their place of residence).
This approximated a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population regarding these demographic markers.

The items of questionnaires that are originally in English and had no German translation available (CRT and CAM) were translated into German by one of the study authors, who's native and second language are German and English.
Translations were then compared to those of the AI-based language translation tool DeepL.
The order of items within all questionnaires was randomized.
All scales used in the study were presented on a 1 to 7 rating scale, keeping the original scale labels.
The full survey can be found on the osf (osf.io/syd5u/) and our translated questionnaires in the supplementary material.
Motivation for Cognition was measured with the Motivation for Cognition (MFC) Scale [22].
text.formatted: Motivation for Cognition was measured with the Motivation for Cognition (MFC) Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: This scale was originally constructed in German and has 10 items (e.g., "Right now, I would really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions to problems.").
Items are scored on a scale of 1 (does not apply at all) to 7 (applies exactly).
Scale reliability was good with Cronbach's α = .85.

Ability for Cognitive Reflection (CR) was measured using the CRT-MQ-4 [44], of which we used six of the original seven Cognitive Reflection Tasks, where we summed up the correct answers to a 7-point scale consistent with the length of the other rating scales.
text.formatted: Ability for Cognitive Reflection (CR) was measured using the CRT-MQ-4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>, of which we used six of the original seven Cognitive Reflection Tasks, where we summed up the correct answers to a 7-point scale consistent with the length of the other rating scales.

text.text: Items had a fouroption multiple choice answer format which contained the correct answer, an intuitive but wrong alternative and two distractors.
(Example item: "Jerry received both the 15th highest and the 15th lowest mark in the class.
How many students are in the class?
"1 = 29 students (correct answer),2 = 30 students (intuitive answer),3 = 1 student,4 = 15 students).
Belief in alternative medicine was measured via the Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) subscale of the larger Holistic Complementary and Alternative Medicine Questionnaire (HCAMQ) [45].
text.formatted: Belief in alternative medicine was measured via the Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) subscale of the larger Holistic Complementary and Alternative Medicine Questionnaire (HCAMQ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref>.

text.text: These six items measure beliefs about the scientific validity of CAM (e.g., "Complementary medicine should only be used as a last resort when conventional medicine has nothing to offer").
Responses to each item were made on a 7-point rating scale ranging from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree".
Items were re-coded in such a way that a high score indicates stronger belief in CAM and a low score rejection of it.
Scale reliability was sufficient with Cronbach's α = .78.

Trust in Science was measured with five items on public trust in scientists [46] (e.g., "Scientists can be trusted because they are experienced experts in their particular topic."), rated on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) scale.
text.formatted: Trust in Science was measured with five items on public trust in scientists <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> (e.g., "Scientists can be trusted because they are experienced experts in their particular topic."), rated on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) scale.

text.text: This scale is originally in German.
Mean scores were calculated, with higher scores indicating greater trust in science.
Scale reliability was excellent with Cronbach's α = .92.
Intellectual Humility was measured with the Intellectual Humility Scale [47].
text.formatted: Intellectual Humility was measured with the Intellectual Humility Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref>.

text.text: This scale measures Intellectual Humility with 6 self-assessed items (e.g., "I am willing to admit it if I don't know something") on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
The scale reliability was good with Cronbach's α = .85.

Conspiracy beliefs were measured with two items [48, 49] (e.g., "Certain significant events have been the result of the activity of a small group who secretly manipulate world events."), rated on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) scale.

text.text: Mean scores were calculated, with higher scores indicating stronger conspiracy beliefs.
Scale reliability was acceptable with Cronbach's α = .74 (correlation of the two items: r = .59, p < .001).

text.text: Participants further reported how often they used different information sources (e.g., science formats, in-depth news reporting, short videos on social media, and AI) and for each health information item whether they had encountered it before.
These variables were preregistered as part of the larger study but are not analyzed in the present paper.
In the main part of the study, participants were presented with short written health information texts, which either contained correct or incorrect information.
A piece of information was regarded as correct if there was sufficient evidence in favor of this claim, and incorrect if there was sufficient evidence against it.
To maintain objectivity, we referred to the independent medical fact-checking project "Medizin Transparent" (medizin-transparent.at) by the University for Continuing Education Krems.
This project is certified by the International Fact Checking Network as well as the European Fact Checking Standards Network (EFCSN).
At the time of material collection there were 608 fact checks available on their website regarding information from the domain of health and medicine that are relevant to the Austrian public.

For each claim, the fact-checking team indicated whether it is true or false and how confident they are in the underlying evidence: high ("yes"/"no"), moderate ("likely yes"/"likely not"), or low ("possibly yes"/"possibly not").
True claims where studies showed small effect sizes received the qualifier "a bit" (e.g., "probably yes, a little bit"), and claims without meaningful studies were labelled "no scientific evidence".

For our study, we only included claims rated with high or moderate confidence in the study results and without the small-effect qualifier, that is, claims rated "yes" or "likely yes" (correct information) and "no" or "likely not" (incorrect information).
At the time of material creation, this left 60 pieces of information that we categorized as correct and 59 that we categorized as incorrect.

From this pool we excluded information regarding impermanent and current medical events such as information regarding the COVID-19 pandemic as well as false information that could do substantial harm if believed (e.g., recommending a natural product such as ginger instead of chemotherapy to treat cancer).
To create the initial texts, we collected 1 to 2 real webpages or articles that displayed the information for each item.

From these, we extracted the main "fact", e.g., "Taking vitamin C regularly prevents the common cold" (incorrect), and between 2 and 3 arguments that explained or supported the fact, e.g., "Vitamin C works as an antioxidant by fighting free radicals".
Based on this material, initial texts were created using ChatGPT [50], using a standardized prompt.
text.formatted: Based on this material, initial texts were created using ChatGPT <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>, using a standardized prompt.

text.text: The texts were then checked and edited by two of the study's authors.
Following this method, we ended up with k = 31 incorrect information texts and k = 35 correct information texts.
We tested these in a prestudy of N = 128 people to select the information pieces for the main study (see complete information on the prestudy in the Supplementary Materials).

According to the prestudy results we excluded the 6 most extreme false items and the 10 most extreme true items, so we ended up with our final item pool of k = 50 stimuli (k = 25 correct and incorrect, each), which covered a large variety of medical and health-related topics.
Participants were presented with the items in a randomized order and answered the following questions after each item: "Do you think this information is true or false?"
(1 = "true",0 = "false"), and "How credible do you think this information is?"
(1 = "not credible at all" to7 = "very credible").
Additionally, we asked participants if they had heard the information before or not, or if they were unsure or heard the opposite (which is not a relevant variable in this paper).
The study was conducted online using LimeSurvey.
Before beginning the study, participants provided informed consent to confirm their voluntary participation and understanding of the study's purpose and procedures.

Participants were then asked to provide demographic information concerning their gender, age, nationality, education, place of residence (rural, small town or city), as well as their political orientation and income.
The study was quotacontrolled, so that participants belonging to an already filled quota could not complete the study.
Following this, participants answered the MFC questionnaire [22] and the CR Test [44].
text.formatted: Following this, participants answered the MFC questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> and the CR Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>.

text.text: This was followed by the main part of the study.
Participants were presented with a total of 50 items of health-related information.
The items appeared one at a time in a randomized order.
After each item, participants were asked the three questions pertaining to veracity, credibility and prior exposure.

After the tenth item, participants performed an attention check, where they were asked which information they had seen on the previous page and had to select the correct answer out of five answer options.
Half of the randomized information items were correct (evidence-based), while the other half were factually incorrect (contrary to the currently available evidence).
After rating all 50 items, participants were presented with the other questionnaires in the following order: CAM-scale, trust in science, intellectual humility, conspiracy belief and media use.
Items for each scale were randomized We further asked participants if and how distracted they were during the study and what device they used.
This was followed by a debriefing about the veracity of the texts, which participants could download for future reference, which linked back to the fact-checking website medizin-transparent.at.
For each participant, an accuracy and a bias score was calculated from the binary health information responses according to a SDT approach.
Each participant's responses towards the items (i.e., health information items) in the experimental part were categorized (Table 1).
text.formatted: Each participant's responses towards the items (i.e., health information items) in the experimental part were categorized (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: For the correct items, "true" responses were categorized as Hits and "false" responses as Misses.
For the incorrect items, "false" responses were categorized as Correct Rejections and "true" responses as False alarms.

text.text: From these we calculated the hit rate (HR = Hits/Number of correct items) and the false alarm rate (FR = False Alarms/ Number of incorrect items).
To avoid extreme rates, we applied a loglinear correction to the False Alarm and Hit Rates by adding 0.5 to each of the cells [51].
text.formatted: To avoid extreme rates, we applied a loglinear correction to the False Alarm and Hit Rates by adding 0.5 to each of the cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref>.

text.text: From these we calculated the accuracy value d', which is defined as the standardized difference between the means of the signal absent and signal present or in this case "evidence based" and "not evidence based" items. d' was calculated as follows (equation 1): where z(x) is the quantile function for z distribution, such as that a proportion of 0.5 is standardized to a z score of 0.

The greater d' the more accurately a person can distinguish between correct and incorrect health information, whereas d' values close to zero indicate an inability to distinguish between the information and a chance performance.

The value for response bias was defined as the criterion value c and corresponds to the individual threshold of responding "true" or "false" to all the information presented. c is calculated using the following equation ( 2 Perceived credibility constituted our secondary dependent variable.
text.formatted: The value for response bias was defined as the criterion value c and corresponds to the individual threshold of responding "true" or "false" to all the information presented. c is calculated using the following equation ( <ref type="formula">2</ref> Perceived credibility constituted our secondary dependent variable.

text.text: It was operationalized using the credibility ratings (1 = "not credible at all" to7 = "very credible"), which were information-adjusted so that higher scores indicate ratings in line with the scientific evidence: ratings of correct items remained unchanged, whereas ratings of incorrect items were reverse-coded (e.g., a rating of 7 for an incorrect item became 1).

To describe how participants responded to correct and incorrect information separately, we additionally classified each participant's HR (proportion of correct items judged as "true") and FR (proportion of incorrect items judged as "true") as below chance, at chance, or above chance, based on the raw proportions.
This was done using the standard error of a proportion (SEprop), which is described in the equation (3): SEprop = √(.5 × .5 / kitems)
Under random guessing and with k = 25 items per category, the SEprop is .10.

Rates within one SE of .50 were therefore treated as chance level: rates ≤ .40 (≤ 10 of 25 items) were coded -1, rates between .41 and .59 (11-14 items) were coded 0, and rates ≥ .60 (≥ 15 items) were coded +1.
For correct information, a hit rate coded +1 indicates performance better than chance (accepting correct information) and -1 performance worse than chance (rejecting it).

For false information, performance is defined by correct rejections: a false alarm rate coded -1 indicates better-than-chance performance (rejecting incorrect information), and a false alarm rate coded +1 worse-than-chance performance (accepting it).

Crossing the three performance levels for correct and for incorrect information resulted in nine groups, ranging from participants who "followed the scientific evidence" (better than chance for both) to those who "responded contrary to it" (worse than chance for both), who "guessed", who are "naive" (accepting everything) and "skeptical" (rejecting everything) in their profiles.
These groups correspond to regions in d′-c space (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: These groups correspond to regions in d′-c space (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2</ref>).

text.text: All analyses were conducted using R [52] and jamovi [53] using the packages GAMLj [54], TOSTER [55], and ggplot2 [56] for figures.
text.formatted: All analyses were conducted using R <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref> and jamovi [53] using the packages GAMLj <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[54]</ref>, TOSTER <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[55]</ref>, and ggplot2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[56]</ref> for figures.

text.text: All statistical tests were conducted two-sided with a significance level of .05.

As preregistered, we calculated general linear models with the individual predictors and the dependent variables accuracy (d') as regression and credibility ratings as multilevel models with trials (i.e., each health information) nested in participants and compared the effect sizes found in the model to the ones used in the power analysis (corresponding to small effect sizes: η² = 0.03, i.e., 3% variance explained; similar to d = 0.34, r = 0.17, β = 0.12, OR = 1.85).

Credibility ratings were analyzed with linear mixed models in which trials (Level 1; N = 17,150) were crossed with participants (N = 343) and items (k = 50), with random intercepts for both participants and items.

Models were estimated via REML with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; all Level 2 predictors as well as the dependent variable were z-standardized, so that fixed effects can be interpreted as standardized coefficients (β).

We performed additional equivalence (TOST) tests on the predictors for accuracy to determine if the correlation between the variables was equivalent to zero, using the equivalence bounds of r = -.17 and r = .17.

text.text: Contrary to our hypothesis, CR was not significantly associated with participants' accuracy (d'), r = .08, 95% CI[-.03, .18], p = .151; the equivalence test was statistically equivalent to zero within Δr ± .17, 90%CI[-.01, .166].
Similarly, MFC also showed no association with accuracy, r = .07, 95% CI[-.03, .18], p = 0.179; the equivalence test was statistically equivalent to zero within Δr ± .17, 90% CI[-0.02, .16].
As hypothesized, participants' CAM was negatively associated with their overall accuracy, r = -.28, 95% CI[-.38, -.18], p < .001.

text.text: When CR, MFC, and CAM were entered simultaneously, the model was significant, R² = .09, F(3, 339) = 11.00, p <.001 (Table 3).
text.formatted: When CR, MFC, and CAM were entered simultaneously, the model was significant, R² = .09, F(3, 339) = 11.00, p <.001 (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: Only CAM predicted accuracy in the hypothesized direction, which we treat as robust evidence for H3: People who held stronger beliefs in alternative medicine were worse at distinguishing true and false health information.
Neither CR nor MFC was a significant predictor.
We observed similar patterns for the information-adjusted credibility ratings (H1b-H3b); where higher values correspond to more appropriate ratings.
We fitted a linear mixed effects model using CR, MFC and CAM as predictors and credibility ratings as the outcome.
The model included random intercepts for participants and items to account for the crossed structure of the data (N = 343, k = 50, 17,150 observations in total).
The model explained 16.4% of the variance conditionally and 0.3% marginally and fit better than the model containing only the participant random intercept, ΔR2 = .158, χ 2 (4) = 2659.02, p <.001.

text.text: Variance was substantially larger for items (σ2 = .155) than for participants (σ2 = .007).
Fixed effects are reported in Table 3.

text.text: CR was not associated with the credibility ratings, CAM had a small negative association, and MFC had a very small positive association in the hypothesized direction.
As this association was not found for accuracy and lies far below the smallest effect size of interest, the evidence for H2b is limited.
To test H4, we added the CAM x CR and CAM x MFC interactions to the accuracy and credibility models (Table 3).
