text.text: Trust in science was positively associated with accuracy, r = .14, 95% CI [.03, .24], p = .010 and with information-adjusted credibility in the same multilevel model, β = .020, SE = 0.010, 95% CI[0.001, 0.039], t(340) = 2.09, p = .038.

Although the point estimate was slightly below our smallest effect size of interest, equivalence to zero could not be established, Δr ± .17, 90% CI[.05, .22], so the association cannot be dismissed as negligible.

In an exploratory robustness check including all individual-difference variables simultaneously, intellectual humility, CAM, and conspiracy belief remained significant predictors of credibility ratings, whereas trust in science did not, and the small association of MFC with credibility ratings (H2b) was no longer significant (β = .018, p = .256) (Supplementary Table S2).

Health misinformation spreads rapidly in online environments, yet it is still not well understood why some people believe incorrect health claims while others do not.

We tested whether the ability and motivation to think effortfully and prior beliefs are related to how well people tell true from false health information (accuracy) and to how readily they accept claims in general (response bias).

To this end, we presented a quota-representative sample of the Austrian population with correct and incorrect health claims based on real online information and analyzed participants' responses using a signal-detection approach.
Contrary to our expectations, CR and MFC were unrelated to accuracy.
Instead, stronger CAM and stronger conspiracy belief were related to lower accuracy.

Trust in science showed a small positive association with accuracy and credibility that did not hold when controlling for the other belief variables, and intellectual humility was unrelated to accuracy.
Participants with stronger CAM, higher trust in science and higher age accepted claims more readily.
Taken together, this speaks against a simple lack-of-reflection account for health misinformation.
Surprisingly, neither the ability nor the motivation to reflect (captured by CR and MFC) was related to accuracy.

This contradicts dual-process accounts, according to which people fall for misinformation because they fail to reflect [7, 17, 18], and contrasts with research on political news, where reflection is often associated with better discernment [16, 17, 40].
text.formatted: This contradicts dual-process accounts, according to which people fall for misinformation because they fail to reflect <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>, and contrasts with research on political news, where reflection is often associated with better discernment <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40]</ref>.

text.text: These findings may therefore not generalize to health information.
One explanation might be that evaluating health information often requires medical and scientific knowledge that most laypeople lack.
Political news, on the other hand, is often part of everyday life and of direct concern for the people.

About half of the Austrian population has limited health literacy [57], finds it difficult to judge whether health information is trustworthy [58], and feels poorly informed about new medical discoveries [59].
text.formatted: About half of the Austrian population has limited health literacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[57]</ref>, finds it difficult to judge whether health information is trustworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[58]</ref>, and feels poorly informed about new medical discoveries <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[59]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, poor truth discernment has been linked not only to a lack of careful reasoning but also to a lack of relevant knowledge [18], and knowledge has been associated with better discrimination between true and fabricated news stories [60].
text.formatted: Similarly, poor truth discernment has been linked not only to a lack of careful reasoning but also to a lack of relevant knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>, and knowledge has been associated with better discrimination between true and fabricated news stories <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[60]</ref>.

text.text: For health misinformation specifically, health literacy consistently predicted susceptibility, whereas cognitive reflection did so only for some health topics and self-reported reflection did not protect against it [31, 61].
text.formatted: For health misinformation specifically, health literacy consistently predicted susceptibility, whereas cognitive reflection did so only for some health topics and self-reported reflection did not protect against it <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">61]</ref>.

text.text: Studies that did find effects of cognitive reflection on health misinformation mostly focused on COVID-19 (e.g., [11, 20, 41]).
text.formatted: Studies that did find effects of cognitive reflection on health misinformation mostly focused on COVID-19 (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>).

text.text: Because this topic received exceptionally extensive media coverage, it might resemble political news more than other health information.

Health information also covers a much wider field and much of it may not be personally relevant (e.g., depending on age, gender, or medical conditions) and may thus give people little reason to think about it carefully, which could explain why motivation for cognition played no role.
Beliefs, in contrast, were by far the strongest predictors of accuracy.

When judging political news, beliefs mainly shift response bias: people are more likely to judge a headline as true when it favors their own political identity, but they are not worse, if anything slightly better, at telling true from false headlines that favor their side [18].
text.formatted: When judging political news, beliefs mainly shift response bias: people are more likely to judge a headline as true when it favors their own political identity, but they are not worse, if anything slightly better, at telling true from false headlines that favor their side <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: In our study, by contrast, participants with stronger belief in CAM and conspiracy theories were worse at distinguishing correct from incorrect health claims.
When people lack the knowledge to evaluate a health claim, they may fall back on what they already believe, even if these beliefs are inaccurate.
Notably, CAM predicted lower accuracy even though the incorrect claims did not particularly focus on alternative medicine.

One possible explanation is that CAM is part of a broader set of beliefs: it is associated with a broader conspiratorial belief system [62]; in our data, too, conspiracy belief was associated with both CAM and lower accuracy.
text.formatted: One possible explanation is that CAM is part of a broader set of beliefs: it is associated with a broader conspiratorial belief system <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[62]</ref>; in our data, too, conspiracy belief was associated with both CAM and lower accuracy.

text.text: We also observed a small interaction: the negative association between CAM and accuracy was slightly stronger for more reflective participants.
This can be explained with motivated reasoning [36], as analytical people tend to show a stronger bias toward belief-congruent information [40].
text.formatted: This can be explained with motivated reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>, as analytical people tend to show a stronger bias toward belief-congruent information <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: Given its small effect size, this interaction should be replicated, ideally with items designed to elicit a stronger belief-related bias.
When reasoning is unhelpful and people have to decide under uncertainty, their general tendency to accept or reject claims becomes important.
Most of our participants showed a liberal response bias, that is, a tendency to judge information as "true" regardless of its veracity.
As half our claims were incorrect, this means that participants accepted many false claims along with the correct ones, and the largest group we identified was characterized by this "naive" tendency.
This suggests a high general susceptibility to health misinformation in the Austrian population, driven mainly by a liberal response bias.
Few studies have examined predictors of response bias in this context, and those that did found no reliable or only weak associations [20, 41].
text.formatted: Few studies have examined predictors of response bias in this context, and those that did found no reliable or only weak associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>.

text.text: In our study, stronger belief in alternative medicine, higher trust in science and higher age were robustly associated with a more liberal response bias.
Stronger CAM was associated not only with lower accuracy but also with a more liberal response bias.

Belief in alternative medicine does not necessarily seem to be related to the rejection of scientific information (which we did not observe in our sample at all) but with a general tendency to accept all health claims, whether scientific or not.
Higher age was also associated with a more liberal response bias.

In line with this, older adults also share considerably more fake news on social media than younger adults [63], possibly because they are less familiar with digital media and with how often false information circulates online [64].
text.formatted: In line with this, older adults also share considerably more fake news on social media than younger adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[63]</ref>, possibly because they are less familiar with digital media and with how often false information circulates online <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[64]</ref>.

text.text: Higher trust in science was likewise associated with a more liberal response bias.
Although increasing trust in science is a common goal in the face of science denial, our study shows that high trust in science can also have adverse effects.
As we observed during material creation, false health claims often borrow scientific authority by referring to studies, using technical language or presenting complex pseudoscientific explanations.
Trust in science without critical evaluation can therefore increase belief in incorrect claims [65].
text.formatted: Trust in science without critical evaluation can therefore increase belief in incorrect claims <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[65]</ref>.

text.text: Complex explanations can even make conspiracy theories more believable [35].
text.formatted: Complex explanations can even make conspiracy theories more believable <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: This means that interventions that merely tell people to look for "scientific credibility cues" (e.g., checking if there is a study quoted) are unlikely to improve discrimination if people lack the knowledge or literacy for critical evaluation.
Because evaluating claims through reasoning requires scientific and medical knowledge, one option would be to improve this knowledge directly.
But given how broad the field of health information is, this hardly seems feasible.
A more realistic approach would be behavioral interventions that change what people do when they encounter health claims.

As people generally tend to accept rather than reject information, such interventions could raise awareness that much online health information may be false and, at the same time, teach people how to find and use verified fact-checking websites, such as medizin-transparent.at in Austria.

Raising awareness alone can increase general skepticism: exposure to fact-checks, tips for spotting fake news or news coverage of misinformation can reduce belief in incorrect claims but also in correct ones [8], and gamified inoculation interventions mainly led people to respond "false" to all news items [66].
text.formatted: Raising awareness alone can increase general skepticism: exposure to fact-checks, tips for spotting fake news or news coverage of misinformation can reduce belief in incorrect claims but also in correct ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, and gamified inoculation interventions mainly led people to respond "false" to all news items <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[66]</ref>.

text.text: This skepticism is not necessarily harmful, however.
Unlike participants in these studies, people who are unsure about a claim can seek out further information before accepting or rejecting it.
Combined with the skills to check claims, a more skeptical stance could thus improve discrimination instead of leading people to dismiss accurate information.

Finally, the response-profile grouping approach used in this study could help to tailor interventions to individuals: for example, people who recognize correct information but guess when judging incorrect information would benefit most from education targeting incorrect claims in particular.

In contrast to most previous research, which used political news or focused on COVID-19, our health-information items covered a wide range of health topics that were not tied to temporary events, which increases the generalizability of our findings.
Some limitations should nonetheless be noted.
First, participants judged each claim in a forced-choice format, without the option to look up further information.

The liberal response bias in particular may therefore partly reflect guessing under uncertainty, which people can avoid outside the experimental setting provided they have the knowledge and motivation to seek out verified information.
Second, our design was correlational, so we have to be careful when interpreting causality.
People who find it difficult to evaluate health information may also be more drawn to alternative medicine or conspiracy theories, or both may depend on a third variable such as health literacy.
Future studies could measure health literacy or medical knowledge to test whether reflection improves accuracy only when relevant knowledge is available.
They could also give participants the option to seek out further information, which would show whether the liberal response bias reflects actual belief or guessing under uncertainty.
Finally, intervention studies could test whether combining awareness of health misinformation with verification skills improves discrimination without increasing general skepticism.

How well people discern correct from incorrect health information is related more to what they believe than to how much they reflect, especially belief in alternative medicine was associated with lower accuracy.
At the same time, most people tend to accept health claims regardless of their veracity, which implies a high general susceptibility to health misinformation.
This tendency was stronger among people with stronger belief in alternative medicine, higher trust in science and higher age.

Rather than encouraging reflection or trust in science, interventions should therefore build on these correlates and teach people how to accurately discriminate health information without undermining trust in accurate information.
